```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Bash chunks are a record of commands you ran in the Terminal. Knitting shows
# them but doesn't run them again.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "bash") options$eval <- FALSE
  options
})
```

Once again, I started by navigating to the proper directory. I made my bins, so it was time to check their quality. Where better to check 'em than in CheckM?
```{bash}
cd ~/bbd-metagenome/checkm
```

For reasons that still don't quite make sense to me, metbat often neglects to bin the longest contig. Because of this, I had to add it in manually. The following code lists out the contigs by lengths. With this data set, I found that the longest contig was contig_138.
```{bash}
cat ../flye/bbd/assembly.fasta | bioawk -c fastx '{print length($seq),$name}' | sort -n
```

Now that I identified contig_138, I used samtools to save it in a bin of its own alongside its siblings, and then copied that whole folder into the checkm folder.
```{bash}
samtools faidx ../flye/bbd/assembly.fasta contig_138 > ..
/metabat/bins_bbd/contig_138.fa
cp ../metabat/bins_bbd/*.fa bins_bbd/
```

I then made a shell script saved as run_checkm_bbd.sh in the checkm folder. This shell contains a slurm script with the following code.
```{bash}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=60
#SBATCH --ntasks=6 --mem=40gb

echo "Starting checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"

shopt -s expand_aliases
alias checkm='apptainer run -B /pvol/:/pvol /pvol/data/sif/checkm.sif checkm'

checkm lineage_wf bins_bbd out -t 6 -x fa -f checkm_results_bbd.txt

echo "Finished checkm in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

Once the code was saved, I pasted the following code into the terminal to submit the script.
```{bash}
sbatch run_checkm_bbd.sh
```

It took quite a while for the servers to get to my request, so the following morning I ran this code to check my results.
```{bash}
head checkm_results_bbd.txt 
```

Finding no results, I checked in with my instructor. As it should happen, the dummy file (ID xx) was preventing my request from being completed. Going into the bins_bbd folder through the files pane in R studio, I manually deleted this blip and resubmitted my request via the code line two blocks up. I ran the following code to stay updated on its progress
```{bash}
tail -f slurm-521.out
```

Once I got the "finished checkm..." message, I ran the following line in the Terminal to view my results.
```{bash}
head checkm_results_bbd.txt 
```

Several parameters were listed, completeness, contamination, and heterogeneity. We can use awk to filter our bins to those with more than 15% completeness, print to specify that we only want to show the ids, and "> [filename]" to output this filtered list as its own file. The code containing these three functions in a single line is as follows.
```{bash}
cat checkm_results_bbd.txt | awk '$13>15{print $1}' > bbd_topbins.txt
```

Having thus created a file, I was ready to move on to the next step, taxonomic classification.

Completeness and contamination of each bin, estimated with CheckM, and selection of the most complete bins for further analysis. Commands for this step were run in `checkm/`.
